title: Mosquitoes Can Learn to Love DEET, Turning Bug Spray Into a Dinner Bell
excerpt: A new study shows lab mosquitoes trained to associate the world's most popular repellent with blood meals began actively seeking out DEET-treated skin — a finding with implications for tropical disease prevention worldwide.
body:
• Researchers found that Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can be conditioned to associate DEET with food, flipping the repellent from aversive to attractive after just four exposures.
  • Trained mosquitoes preferred DEET-treated human hands over untreated ones, raising concerns about fading repellent creating a window of vulnerability.
  • Scientists say the study reinforces the importance of reapplying DEET regularly, rather than relying on a single application.
  • The findings could spur development of next-generation repellents to complement DEET, critical for regions where mosquito-borne diseases remain endemic.

Mosquitoes, already the world's deadliest animal, may have another trick: learning to seek out the very chemical designed to repel them. A study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology demonstrates that Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can be trained through Pavlovian conditioning to associate DEET — the active ingredient in most commercial bug sprays — with a blood meal, ultimately flipping their natural aversion into active attraction.

The research, led by Clément Vinauger, an associate professor of biochemistry at Virginia Tech, and Claudio Lazzari at the University of Tours in France, challenges a long-held assumption that DEET works as a simple chemical barrier mosquitoes cannot overcome.

"Mosquitoes are very smart and can outsmart our control tools. DEET is a molecule that can be interpreted by the mosquito brain, and mosquitoes can learn to like it."

— Clément Vinauger, Virginia Tech

How the Experiment Worked

The team exposed female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to the odour of DEET while simultaneously offering them a blood meal through a heated artificial feeder. After four conditioning sessions, more than 60 percent of the trained mosquitoes extended their proboscis — the needle-like mouthpart used for feeding — when presented with the DEET scent alone, even without blood present.

The effect held when sugar replaced blood as the reward, suggesting the learning mechanism is broadly applicable across food sources.

The researchers then tested whether this laboratory conditioning translated to more realistic scenarios. Trained mosquitoes were offered a choice between two human hands positioned behind a mesh barrier — one treated with DEET, the other untreated. The conditioned insects showed a clear preference for the DEET-treated hand, approaching it more readily and probing more often.

"The general consensus was that repellents worked solely because of their chemical properties: either they were toxic or unpleasant to mosquitoes, driving them away, or they blocked their ability to detect humans," Lazzari told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. The new findings upend that consensus.

What This Means in the Real World

The researchers caution that the study represents a controlled laboratory scenario, and it remains unclear how frequently such conditioning occurs in natural settings. However, they outline a plausible real-world pathway.

"If someone applies DEET and the concentration fades over time, but a mosquito still manages to feed, the insect may begin associating that smell with a reward," Vinauger said. "That's a possibility we should take seriously when we think about how repellents are used in the real world."

Lazzari elaborated on the mechanism: when a person applies DEET hours before a mosquito encounter and the concentration drops below the repellent threshold while the scent lingers, a mosquito that successfully feeds could form a positive association with the chemical. That mosquito may then preferentially target other DEET-wearing individuals.

The practical takeaway is straightforward — reapply insect repellent as often as label directions indicate, rather than relying on a single morning application to last through the evening.

Stakes for India and the Diaspora

The findings carry particular weight for Indians at home and abroad. India accounts for a significant share of the global dengue burden, and diseases like malaria, chikungunya, and Zika remain persistent threats, especially during the monsoon season. DEET-based repellents are a frontline defence for the millions of diaspora members who travel to India annually to visit family, and for residents in high-transmission zones.

If mosquitoes in endemic regions are learning to overcome DEET through repeated sub-lethal exposure — a scenario the researchers say is plausible — it could weaken a critical layer of personal protection in areas where healthcare infrastructure is already strained.

Toward Smarter Repellents

Vinauger's lab at Virginia Tech has spent years mapping how mosquitoes process sensory information. Previous work from his team showed that mosquitoes can remember and avoid hosts who swat at them, and that they combine smell and vision to track people with surprising precision.

The DEET study fits into a broader push to understand mosquito cognition, not just chemistry. "We need to understand how mosquitoes keep outsmarting our control strategies," Vinauger said. "And that takes understanding of how they work — at the molecular level, the neural level, the behavioural level."

Separately, a study published in Nature Communications by a Baylor University-led team identified a specific sensory receptor, OR49, that Aedes aegypti use to detect and avoid borneol, a compound found in camphor and rosemary. When researchers genetically disabled OR49, the mosquitoes lost their ability to avoid the compound — a finding that could inform the design of repellents that target hardwired avoidance pathways rather than relying on learned behaviour.

Together, the two lines of research suggest the next generation of mosquito control will need to be as adaptive as the insects themselves, combining chemical deterrents with a deeper understanding of how mosquito brains learn, remember, and decide.
